subject: Government
title: Colonial Administration Systems
outline: British colonial policy and Indirect Rule
Machinery of Indirect Rule in Nigeria
Successes and failures of Indirect Rule by region
French policy of Assimilation and Association
Comparison of British and French systems

modules.title: British Indirect Rule
modules.html:
1. Meaning

Indirect Rule was the British system of administering colonies through existing traditional rulers and institutions, supervised by British officials. Introduced in Northern Nigeria by Lord Frederick Lugard from 1900 and extended to the South after the 1914 amalgamation.

2. Machinery

ComponentRole
Governor-GeneralOverall head of the colony and protectorate
Lieutenant-Governors / Chief CommissionersHeaded the groups of provinces (North, South)
ResidentsSupervised a province and advised the Emir/Native Authority
District OfficersSupervised divisions and native courts
Native AuthorityTraditional ruler-in-council exercising local executive power
Native Treasury (Beit-el-mal)Kept a share of local revenue for local administration
Native CourtsApplied customary and Islamic law in local disputes

3. Reasons for Adoption

  1. Shortage of British personnel and funds.
  2. Vastness of territory and poor communications.
  3. Existence of well-organised traditional authorities, especially in the North.
  4. Desire to avoid resistance by preserving familiar institutions.
  5. Language and cultural barriers.
  6. Belief in gradual, evolutionary development of Africans.

4. Regional Outcomes

  • North: highly successful — the emirate hierarchy, taxation and Alkali courts fitted the model. Christian missions and Western education were restricted, widening the North–South educational gap.
  • West: partially successful — Obas existed but were constitutionally limited by chiefs and cults; educated elites and a vocal press resisted, and the 1918 Adubi war and Egba unrest showed strain.
  • East: largely a failure — no centralised chiefs, so warrant chiefs were imposed. Their abuses provoked the 1929 Aba Women's Riot, after which the system was reformed.

5. Merits and Demerits

Merits: cheap, preserved traditional institutions, minimised friction, trained locals in administration, maintained order. Demerits: strengthened autocratic chiefs beyond custom, excluded educated elites, retarded political development and education in the North, entrenched regional disparities, and made chiefs unpopular as agents of colonial taxation.

examples.q: Why did educated Nigerians oppose Indirect Rule?
examples.a: Because it excluded them. The system reserved authority for hereditary chiefs whom the British could control, while lawyers, journalists and teachers — the very people equipped to demand representation — were kept out of the Native Authorities. Nationalists such as Herbert Macaulay and later Azikiwe therefore argued it was designed to divide the elite from the masses and delay self-government.

examples.q: State two lasting consequences of the 1914 amalgamation.
examples.a: (i) It created a single Nigerian state out of the Northern and Southern Protectorates and Lagos Colony for administrative and financial convenience — using the South's surplus to fund the North — without integrating their peoples, leaving a legacy of North–South suspicion. (ii) It preserved separate administrative systems and educational policies, entrenching the developmental imbalance that later shaped constitutional bargaining, regionalism and revenue allocation disputes.

modules.title: French Assimilation and Association, and Comparison
modules.html:
1. Assimilation

French policy from the late nineteenth century aimed to turn Africans into Frenchmen: French language, law, culture and citizenship were extended, and the colonies were treated as overseas extensions of France. Four communes of Senegal (Dakar, Goree, Rufisque and Saint-Louis) elected a deputy to the French Parliament in Paris. Africans who met the criteria became evolues, full citizens; others remained sujets subject to the harsh indigenat code and forced labour.

Reasons for failure: costly; cultural arrogance provoked resentment; the mass of Africans could never qualify; French settlers and businessmen opposed African equality; assimilation of millions would have swamped the French Parliament.

2. Association

After 1900 France shifted to Association: cooperation with African institutions while keeping ultimate French control, with more use of chiefs (though chiefs were appointed officials, not traditional rulers) and recognition of some African custom. It remained highly centralised through Governors-General at Dakar and Brazzaville.

3. Comparison

CriterionBritish Indirect RuleFrench Assimilation/Association
PhilosophyPreserve African institutions; gradual self-governmentAbsorb Africans into French civilisation; permanent union
AdministrationDecentralised; through traditional rulersHighly centralised from Paris via Dakar
Role of chiefsTraditional rulers retained real authorityChiefs were paid agents, removable at will
LawCustomary and Islamic law retained in native courtsFrench law imposed; indigenat for subjects
CitizenshipColonial subjects; no British citizenshipCitizenship possible for evolues
RepresentationLegislative councils in the colonyDeputies in the French Parliament
OutcomeFederal, English-speaking states with strong local identityUnitary, French-oriented states tied closely to France

examples.q: Why did the four communes matter in French colonial history?
examples.a: They were the only African territories where the assimilation ideal was substantially realised: their inhabitants were French citizens with the right to elect a deputy to the National Assembly in Paris. Blaise Diagne's election in 1914 as the first African deputy proved Africans could operate French institutions, and became a reference point for later demands for equality throughout French West Africa.

examples.q: Which system better prepared colonies for independence?
examples.a: Indirect Rule preserved local institutions and produced legislative councils that evolved into national parliaments, giving Nigerians earlier experience of representative politics; but it neglected mass education and entrenched regionalism. Assimilation produced a small, highly trained elite closely tied to France with weak local institutions. Neither prepared colonies fully; the British model transferred more institutional machinery, the French model more administrative centralisation.

modules.title: Successes and failures of Indirect Rule by region
modules.html:
Successes and failures of Indirect Rule by region is a key part of Colonial Administration Systems (SSS 3, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Meaning Indirect Rule was the British system of administering colonies through existing traditional rulers and institutions, supervised by British officials.
  • Machinery Component Role Governor-General Overall head of the colony and protectorate Lieutenant-Governors / Chief Commissioners Headed the groups of provinces (North, South) Residents Supervised a province and advised the Emir/Native Authority District Officers Supervised divisions and native courts Native Authority Traditional ruler-in-council exercising local executive power Native Treasury (Beit-el-mal) Kept a share of local revenue for local administration Native Courts Applied customary and Islamic law in local disputes 3.
  • Regional Outcomes North: highly successful — the emirate hierarchy, taxation and Alkali courts fitted the model.
  • Demerits: strengthened autocratic chiefs beyond custom, excluded educated elites, retarded political development and education in the North, entrenched regional disparities, and made chiefs unpopular as agents of colonial taxation.
  • Association After 1900 France shifted to Association : cooperation with African institutions while keeping ultimate French control, with more use of chiefs (though chiefs were appointed officials, not traditional rulers) and recognition of some African custom.

Worked example

Q: Indirect Rule in Nigeria is associated with:
A: Lord Lugard — Lugard introduced and systematised Indirect Rule from 1900 in the North.

Q: Indirect Rule failed most in:
A: Eastern Nigeria — The absence of centralised chiefs in Igboland led to the imposition of warrant chiefs.

examples.q: Indirect Rule in Nigeria is associated with:
examples.a: Lord Lugard — Lugard introduced and systematised Indirect Rule from 1900 in the North.
Eastern Nigeria — The absence of centralised chiefs in Igboland led to the imposition of warrant chiefs.

modules.title: Amalgamation of 1914 and its consequences
modules.html:
Amalgamation of 1914 and its consequences is a key part of Colonial Administration Systems (SSS 3, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Introduced in Northern Nigeria by Lord Frederick Lugard from 1900 and extended to the South after the 1914 amalgamation.
  • Lugard amalgamated the protectorates on 1 January 1914.
  • Blaise Diagne was elected in 1914 from the four communes.

Worked example

Q: Amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria occurred in:
A: 1914 — Lugard amalgamated the protectorates on 1 January 1914.

Q: The first African deputy elected to the French Parliament was:
A: Blaise Diagne — Blaise Diagne was elected in 1914 from the four communes.

examples.a: 1914 — Lugard amalgamated the protectorates on 1 January 1914.

examples.q: The first African deputy elected to the French Parliament was:
examples.a: Blaise Diagne — Blaise Diagne was elected in 1914 from the four communes.
